data.content_ref: inline:The target asserts that Popper's reliance on a 'rational faith' costs him 'the claim that his system is purely logical.' But Popper never made that claim in the relevant sense. In 'The Logic of Scientific Discovery,' Popper explicitly states that science rests on methodological conventions or 'rules of the game of science' that are not themselves logical consequences of formal logic — e.g., rules about how to treat falsification, how to select severe tests, etc. He distinguished the deductive logical core (modus tollens, falsifiability) from the methodological superstructure (conventional rules adopted for their fruitfulness in promoting critical discussion). Because Popper openly acknowledged that his system is not 'purely logical' but combines logic with conventions, the target is refuting a claim Popper never held. The target thereby commits a straw-man fallacy: it presents the existence of a non-logical, non-ethical methodological layer as a devastating 'cost,' when Popper treated it as an explicit, advertised feature of his philosophy. This is a distinct flaw from the prior criticism (which addressed the false dichotomy between ethics and pragmatism), because this objection targets the target's meta-claim about what Popper 'loses,' showing it attacks a position Popper did not occupy.
